title: Thiamine and Alcohol: How Drinking Drains Vitamin B1
excerpt: Does alcohol deplete thiamine? How drinking blocks vitamin B1 absorption, who really runs low, whether thiamine helps a hangover, how much to take, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: How alcohol blocks thiamine (vitamin B1) absorption, who actually runs low, whether B1 helps a hangover, how much to take, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol lowers your thiamine (vitamin B1) in several ways at once. It makes your gut absorb less of it, makes your liver store less of it, makes your cells worse at turning it into its working form, and pushes more of it out in your urine. For a social drinker who eats a normal diet, the occasional night out is very unlikely to leave you deficient. The people who really run low are those who drink heavily most days, especially when drinking replaces meals. Thiamine supplements are cheap and very safe, but there is no good evidence that thiamine prevents or relieves a hangover.

**The quick rules:** If you drink a few times a week and eat reasonably well, food or a basic B-complex covers you. If you drink heavily most days, have cut way back on food, have had weight-loss surgery, or take a water pill like furosemide, talk to a doctor about thiamine, because your need may be higher than a multivitamin covers. And if a heavy drinker suddenly becomes confused, unsteady on their feet, or develops odd eye movements or double vision, that is a medical emergency, not a supplement question.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and official nutrition guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor if** you drink heavily on most days, have numbness, tingling, or burning in your feet or hands, have lost a lot of weight or are eating very little, have had bariatric surgery, or take diuretics. **Go to the emergency room or call 911 if** someone who drinks heavily becomes newly confused, can't walk steadily, has jerky or stuck eye movements, double vision, or drooping eyelids, or seems very drowsy and hard to wake. These can be signs of a serious brain condition caused by severe thiamine deficiency, and it needs IV thiamine in a hospital, quickly.

## What Thiamine Does (and Why Your Body Can't Afford to Run Low)

Thiamine is vitamin B1. It was the first B vitamin to be identified, which is why it got the number one. Your body can't make it, so it has to come from food or supplements.

Its main job is helping your cells turn food into usable energy. Once inside a cell, thiamine is converted into its active form, **thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)**, sometimes called thiamine diphosphate. TPP works as a helper (a "cofactor") for several key enzymes that break down glucose and produce energy. Without enough TPP, those energy pathways slow down.

That matters most for the organs that burn the most energy:

- **The brain and nerves**, which run almost entirely on glucose and are very sensitive to a drop in thiamine.
- **The heart**, which never stops working.
- **Muscles**, especially during activity.

Here's the catch that makes alcohol such a problem: your body keeps only a small reserve of thiamine. Estimates put the total store at roughly 25 to 30 mg in an adult, and it turns over quickly. Because the reserve is so small and the vitamin is water-soluble (excess leaves in urine rather than being stored in fat), a few weeks of poor intake can start to run it down. That's why thiamine deficiency can show up faster than deficiencies of vitamins your body hoards, like B12.

### How much do you actually need?

The US National Institutes of Health's Office of Dietary Supplements lists the recommended daily intake for adults as:

| Group | Recommended daily thiamine |
|---|---|
| Adult men | 1.2 mg |
| Adult women | 1.1 mg |
| Pregnant or breastfeeding | 1.4 mg |

These are small amounts, and most people who eat a varied diet get them easily. No upper limit has been set, because no harm has been reported from high intakes of thiamine from food or supplements taken by mouth. That's part of why doctors are comfortable recommending it to people who drink heavily.

## How Alcohol Lowers Thiamine: Five Ways at Once

Researchers have studied the link between alcohol and thiamine since at least the 1970s, and the picture is consistent. Alcohol doesn't just "use up" thiamine. It hits the vitamin at almost every step of its journey through your body.

### 1. Less gets absorbed from your gut

This is the big one, and it's the part people searching "thiamine and alcohol absorption" usually want explained.

Thiamine from food is absorbed mainly in the first part of the small intestine. At normal dietary amounts, it doesn't just leak through the gut wall. It's carried in by **specific transporter proteins** in the cells lining your intestine, a bit like a turnstile that lets thiamine through one molecule at a time.

Lab and animal research has shown that alcohol interferes with those transporters. It reduces how much thiamine the gut cells take in and how efficiently they pass it on into the blood. Studies in people who drink heavily have also found that they absorb noticeably less thiamine from a given dose than people who don't.

There's a useful twist here. At **high doses**, thiamine can also cross the gut wall by simple diffusion, without needing the transporter. That's one reason doctors often use larger oral doses (well above the daily requirement) for people who drink heavily, and why hospitals give it by IV when the stakes are high. More thiamine in the gut can partly make up for a jammed turnstile.

### 2. Your liver stores less of it

The liver holds a good share of the body's thiamine. Regular heavy drinking damages liver cells and can lead to fatty liver, inflammation, and eventually scarring. A damaged liver holds less thiamine, so your already small reserve gets even smaller.

### 3. Your cells are worse at activating it

Thiamine doesn't work until it's been converted to TPP inside your cells. The enzyme that does this conversion needs magnesium, and heavy drinking commonly lowers magnesium too. Research also suggests alcohol interferes with this activation step more directly. So even the thiamine that does make it into your body may not be turned into its working form efficiently.

This magnesium link is easy to miss. Someone can be given thiamine and still not respond well if their magnesium is very low, which is why doctors often check and replace both.

### 4. More leaves in your urine

Alcohol makes you pee more by suppressing a hormone (vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone) that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. Water-soluble vitamins like thiamine get flushed out along with that extra fluid. There's also evidence that alcohol reduces how well the kidneys reabsorb thiamine. For more on the fluid side of this, see our guide on [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking).

### 5. Drinking replaces food

This one isn't chemistry, but it may matter most. Alcohol has calories but essentially no vitamins. When someone drinks heavily, alcohol often stands in for meals. Skipped dinners, a reliance on fast food, or poor appetite the next day all mean less thiamine coming in at the exact time the body is absorbing and keeping less of it.

### Putting it together

Each of these effects on its own might be manageable. Together they explain why thiamine deficiency is one of the best-known nutritional problems linked to long-term heavy drinking. Lower intake, poorer absorption, weaker storage, less activation, and more loss all push in the same direction.

## Does One Night of Drinking Deplete Thiamine?

Not in any way that matters for most people.

A single evening of drinking can temporarily reduce how much thiamine you absorb from whatever you eat that night, and you'll lose a bit more in your urine. But your body's reserve covers short gaps, and as long as you go back to eating normally, you replace it within days. There's no good evidence that an occasional night out causes a meaningful thiamine shortfall in a healthy person who eats a varied diet.

The real risk builds over weeks and months. It's the combination of **frequent heavy drinking** and **eating poorly** that drains the reserve faster than it's replaced. That's why the medical concern about thiamine focuses on people who drink heavily on most days, not on someone who has a few drinks on a Saturday.

## Who Is Most Likely to Run Low

Your risk of low thiamine goes up if you:

- **Drink heavily on most days**, or have long stretches of daily drinking
- **Eat very little** or skip meals when you drink, or have lost weight without trying
- **Vomit often**, whether from drinking or from another cause such as severe morning sickness
- **Have had bariatric (weight-loss) surgery**, which can sharply reduce absorption
- **Take loop diuretics** such as furosemide (Lasix) for heart failure or fluid retention, which increase thiamine loss in urine
- **Have diabetes**, where some research has found lower thiamine levels, partly from higher urinary loss
- **Are older and eat a limited diet**

If two or more of these apply to you, it's worth raising thiamine with your doctor, even if you don't feel any symptoms.

## Signs of Low Thiamine

Mild thiamine deficiency is vague and easy to mistake for something else, including the general rundown feeling that can come with regular drinking. Early signs can include:

- Tiredness and low energy
- Irritability or low mood
- Poor appetite
- Trouble concentrating or memory lapses

As it becomes more serious, thiamine deficiency (historically called **beriberi**) affects the nerves and heart:

- **Nerve symptoms ("dry" beriberi):** tingling, burning, or numbness in the feet and hands, muscle weakness, and cramps, often starting in the legs
- **Heart symptoms ("wet" beriberi):** a fast heartbeat, shortness of breath, and swelling in the legs

Several of these overlap with other conditions, including alcohol's own direct effect on nerves. Numbness or burning in the feet in someone who drinks regularly is worth a doctor's visit, because the cause can be a mix of things and treatment depends on finding it.

### The emergency version: a see-a-doctor note

Severe thiamine deficiency can affect the brain in a condition called **Wernicke's encephalopathy**. The classic signs are confusion, an unsteady, wide-legged walk, and problems with eye movements (jerky eyes, double vision, or eyes that don't move together). Not everyone has all three, and it can be mistaken for being drunk.

This is a medical emergency. It's treated in hospital with high-dose IV thiamine, and fast treatment matters because, if it's missed, it can lead to lasting memory problems. If someone who drinks heavily shows these signs, **go to the emergency room or call 911.** Don't try to handle it with supplements at home.

## Does Thiamine Help a Hangover?

This is the question a lot of people actually have when they look up thiamine and alcohol. The honest answer: **there is no good evidence that thiamine prevents or relieves a hangover.**

Here's what we know and don't know:

- **No good trials test it.** We aren't aware of any well-designed human trial showing that taking thiamine before or after drinking reduces hangover symptoms.
- **Hangover remedies in general are poorly supported.** A systematic review published in the *BMJ* in 2005 looked at the available trials of hangover remedies and found no compelling evidence that any of them worked. Research has improved since then, but B1 hasn't emerged as a proven option.
- **Some diet research points elsewhere.** A 2019 study by Verster and colleagues, which looked at what people ate and how bad their hangovers were, found that higher dietary intake of zinc and nicotinic acid (vitamin B3) was linked to less severe hangovers. That kind of study shows an association, not cause and effect, and it doesn't single out thiamine.
- **The mechanism doesn't line up well.** A hangover is mostly driven by things like dehydration, poor sleep, inflammation, low blood sugar, and the effects of acetaldehyde (the toxic by-product made when your body breaks down alcohol). A short-term dip in thiamine isn't thought to be a main driver.

So why do hangover products so often include B1? Partly because B vitamins are cheap, safe, and sound plausible, and partly because the long-term link between heavy drinking and thiamine deficiency is real, even though that's a different problem from a hangover. Including thiamine in a "morning after" product isn't harmful, but you shouldn't expect it to do the heavy lifting.

If you want a broader look at which vitamins have any hangover evidence, our [vitamins for hangover guide](/never-hungover/vitamins-for-hangover) covers B vitamins, vitamin C, zinc, and more. For a wider view of supplements, see our [hangover supplements guide](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025).

## Should You Take Thiamine if You Drink?

It depends on how much you drink and how you eat.

**If you drink socially and eat a varied diet:** you probably don't need a dedicated thiamine supplement. Your food likely covers the 1.1 to 1.2 mg a day you need. If you want some insurance, a standard multivitamin or B-complex will usually provide at least the daily requirement, often more. That's a reasonable, low-cost choice, but it isn't something to expect a noticeable effect from.

**If you drink heavily most days:** this is where thiamine really matters, and it's worth talking to a doctor rather than guessing. Many doctors recommend thiamine for people who drink heavily because the downside is so small and the deficiency it guards against is serious. Because absorption is reduced, the doses used in this situation are often well above the daily requirement. Your doctor can also check whether you're low in related nutrients, such as magnesium and folate.

**If you're cutting back after a period of heavy drinking:** stopping suddenly after long-term daily heavy drinking can cause withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Shakes, sweating, a racing heart, anxiety, or seeing or hearing things that aren't there after you stop drinking are signs to get medical help. Doctors routinely give thiamine as part of that care, which is another reason to involve them rather than doing it alone.

### Thiamine HCl vs benfotiamine

You'll see two main forms on supplement shelves:

- **Thiamine hydrochloride (thiamine HCl) or thiamine mononitrate.** These are the standard, water-soluble forms used in most multivitamins, B-complexes, and fortified foods. They're cheap and well studied.
- **Benfotiamine.** This is a fat-soluble, man-made form that the body converts to thiamine. It's absorbed differently, without relying as heavily on the gut transporters that alcohol interferes with, and studies show it raises thiamine levels in the blood more than the same dose of regular thiamine. It has been studied mainly for diabetic nerve pain, with mixed results, and there's some small-scale research in people who drink heavily.

For most people, plain thiamine is fine. Benfotiamine is a reasonable option to ask your doctor about if you're specifically concerned about absorption, but there's no good evidence that it does anything for hangovers.

### Timing and how to take it

- **With food is fine.** Thiamine can be taken with or without food. Taking it with a meal may be easier on the stomach if you're taking a multi-ingredient product.
- **Spread out beats saving it all for the morning after.** Because your body doesn't store much, a steady daily intake matters more than one big dose after a night out.
- **Skip the "pre-loading" idea.** Taking a big dose of B1 right before drinking won't stop alcohol from affecting your absorption that night, and it won't prevent a hangover.

### Side effects and interactions

Oral thiamine is one of the safest supplements there is. Side effects at normal supplement doses are rare. It can turn your urine bright yellow, but that's usually from riboflavin (B2) in B-complex products, not thiamine itself.

A few things worth knowing:

- **Loop diuretics** like furosemide increase thiamine loss, so people on them may need more.
- **Some chemotherapy drugs** can interfere with thiamine. If you're being treated for cancer, ask your care team before adding supplements.
- **Allergic reactions** are very rare and have mostly been reported with IV thiamine given in hospital, not oral tablets.

If you take prescription medications, a pharmacist can quickly check your full list. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) also covers common supplement-and-medication questions.

## Getting Thiamine From Food

For most people, food is the best source. Good options include:

| Food | Why it's a good source |
|---|---|
| Pork (chops, tenderloin, ham) | One of the richest natural sources of thiamine |
| Fortified breakfast cereals | Often provide much or all of the daily amount per serving |
| Enriched bread, rice, and pasta | Thiamine is added back during processing in the US and many other countries |
| Beans, lentils, and peas | Good plant-based sources, plus fiber |
| Fish such as trout and salmon | Provide thiamine alongside protein |
| Sunflower seeds, flaxseed, and macadamias | Handy snacks with useful amounts |
| Whole grains like oats and brown rice | Keep more of their natural thiamine |

A few things lower the thiamine you get from food:

- **Raw fish and shellfish** contain an enzyme called thiaminase that breaks down thiamine. Cooking destroys it. This is rarely a problem in a normal diet.
- **Very large amounts of tea or coffee** contain compounds that can interfere with thiamine, though this mostly matters when intake is already low.
- **Heat and water** can wash thiamine out of food. Boiling vegetables and discarding the water loses some; steaming or using the cooking liquid keeps more.

The practical takeaway: if you drink, one of the most useful things you can do is **eat a real meal**. A plate of pork, rice, and beans before going out does more for your thiamine than a capsule taken on an empty stomach at midnight. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers eating, pacing, and hydration habits that do have support.

## Thiamine and the Other B Vitamins

Thiamine rarely runs low on its own. People who drink heavily and eat poorly often run low on several nutrients at once, especially:

- **Folate (B9)**, which alcohol also reduces absorption of
- **Vitamin B6**, which alcohol breaks down faster
- **Magnesium**, which thiamine needs to work
- **Zinc**

That's why doctors often prefer a B-complex or a multivitamin over thiamine alone for people who drink regularly, and why they check several levels at once if they suspect a problem. Taking one isolated B vitamin in large doses doesn't fix a broader nutrition gap.

## A Note on Thiamine and Your Liver and Brain

You'll sometimes see thiamine marketed as "brain protection" for drinkers. There's a real basis for the concern and a lot of overstatement in the marketing.

The real part: long-term heavy drinking is linked to brain and nerve damage, and thiamine deficiency is one well-understood contributor. Keeping thiamine levels normal is a sensible part of reducing that risk. Our article on [alcohol and cognitive decline](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-cognitive-decline-2025-brain-research-reveals-hidden-risks) goes into what the research says.

The overstatement: there is no good evidence that taking extra thiamine lets you drink heavily without harm. Thiamine helps prevent one specific deficiency. It doesn't neutralize alcohol, protect your liver from alcohol's direct effects, or reverse damage that's already happened. Cutting back on how much and how often you drink is still what matters most.

## Where DHM Fits In

If you're reading about thiamine because you want to feel better after drinking, it helps to know what each supplement is actually for.

- **Thiamine** is about preventing a vitamin deficiency, which matters mostly for people who drink heavily over time. It's not a hangover remedy.
- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with only a small amount of human data. It's promising but unproven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in people. It doesn't replace thiamine or a decent diet, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe.

The two aren't in competition, and some hangover products combine DHM with B vitamins. If you want to try DHM, a commonly chosen option is [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), and a lower-cost single-ingredient pick is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If liver health is your main concern, our [milk thistle and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/milk-thistle-and-alcohol) and [best liver supplements roundup](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements) give an honest view of the evidence.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol lowers thiamine by reducing absorption in the gut, storage in the liver, activation in cells, and reabsorption in the kidneys, and by replacing food.
- Your body stores only a small amount of thiamine, so poor intake plus heavy drinking can drain it within weeks.
- For a social drinker who eats well, the occasional night out isn't a real thiamine threat. Food, or a basic multivitamin or B-complex, covers it.
- For people who drink heavily most days, thiamine is genuinely important and worth discussing with a doctor, often alongside magnesium and other B vitamins.
- There is no good evidence that thiamine prevents or cures a hangover.
- Confusion, unsteady walking, or eye-movement problems in a heavy drinker are an emergency. Go to the ER.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol deplete thiamine?**

Yes. Alcohol lowers thiamine in several ways: it reduces how much the gut absorbs, lowers how much the liver can store, interferes with converting thiamine into its active form, increases loss in urine, and often replaces food that would supply it. For occasional social drinkers who eat well, the effect is small and temporary. The serious depletion happens with frequent heavy drinking, especially combined with poor eating.

**How does alcohol affect thiamine absorption?**

Thiamine from food is absorbed mainly through specific transporter proteins in the lining of the small intestine. Research shows alcohol interferes with these transporters, so less thiamine gets into the blood from the same amount of food. At high doses, thiamine can also cross the gut wall by simple diffusion, which is one reason doctors use larger doses for people who drink heavily.

**Does thiamine help with hangovers?**

There is no good evidence that thiamine prevents or relieves a hangover. We aren't aware of any well-designed trial showing a benefit, and hangovers are driven mainly by dehydration, poor sleep, inflammation, and acetaldehyde rather than a short-term dip in B1. Thiamine is safe and cheap, so including it in a B-complex isn't harmful, but don't rely on it to fix how you feel the next morning.

**How much thiamine should I take if I drink alcohol?**

The recommended daily intake for adults is 1.2 mg for men and 1.1 mg for women, which most people who drink socially get from food or a standard multivitamin. People who drink heavily most days often need more because they absorb less, and doctors commonly recommend higher doses in that situation. Ask a doctor for a dose that fits your drinking, diet, and health.

**Is it safe to take thiamine with alcohol?**

Yes. There's no harmful interaction between thiamine and alcohol, and oral thiamine is one of the safest supplements available, with no upper limit set because no harm has been reported from high oral intakes. The issue isn't safety but effectiveness: thiamine doesn't reduce alcohol's effects or prevent a hangover.

**Is benfotiamine better than thiamine for drinkers?**

Benfotiamine is a fat-soluble form that the body converts to thiamine. It raises blood thiamine levels more than the same dose of regular thiamine and relies less on the gut transporters alcohol interferes with. That makes it a reasonable option to ask your doctor about if absorption is a concern. For most people, standard thiamine works fine, and neither form has good evidence for hangovers.

**What are the signs of thiamine deficiency from drinking?**

Early signs are vague: tiredness, irritability, poor appetite, and trouble concentrating. More serious deficiency can cause tingling, burning, or numbness in the feet and hands, muscle weakness, a fast heartbeat, and leg swelling, which are worth a doctor's visit. Sudden confusion, an unsteady walk, or eye-movement problems in someone who drinks heavily are an emergency and need hospital care right away.

**What foods are high in thiamine?**

Pork is one of the richest sources. Fortified breakfast cereals, enriched bread, rice, and pasta, beans and lentils, trout and salmon, sunflower seeds, and whole grains like oats are also good sources. Eating a proper meal before or on days you drink is one of the simplest ways to keep thiamine topped up.
